course.title: The Roman Republic
course.description: From the end of the kings to Augustus, read through the people who wrote about it. Each lesson uses one stretch of Roman history to practise a skill from the History course: reading a source for its purpose, weighing a later account, separating cause from condition, and telling change from continuity.
course.audience: A curious adult who may have done the History course and wants a period to apply it to. They know that Rome had kings, a Republic and emperors, and may have heard of Hannibal and Caesar, but they have not read the ancient writers or asked who wrote each account and why.

paragraphs: From the end of the kings to Augustus, read through the people who wrote about it. Each lesson uses one stretch of Roman history to practise a skill from the History course: reading a source for its purpose, weighing a later account, separating cause from condition, and telling change from continuity.
outcomes: You'll be able to say what Livy, Polybius, Sallust, Caesar, Plutarch and Augustus each wrote for, and weigh what each can tell us.
You'll be able to tell a founding tradition from evidence for the events it describes.
You'll be able to say which body held which power under the Republic's constitution, and how the Struggle of the Orders changed it.
You'll be able to separate the conditions, causes and trigger of the Second Punic War, and read a casualty figure for who counted it.
You'll be able to compare two explanations of why the Republic broke down and say what each could see from where its writer stood.
You'll be able to put the main events from 509 BCE to 27 BCE in order and work out the intervals between them.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on History: How the Past Is Known.

modules.title: Founding and constitution
modules.description: What the Romans said about their beginnings, how a Greek observer described the Republic's offices, and how the first written laws came out of a quarrel between the orders.

modules.title: Italy and Carthage
modules.description: How Rome came to rule Italy, why it went to war with Carthage a second time, and what the accounts of Hannibal's victories can and cannot tell us.

modules.title: Empire and reform
modules.description: What conquest did to the city and the army, read through writers who disagree about why, with the Gracchi, Marius and Sulla as the cases.

modules.title: The end of the Republic
modules.description: Catiline, Cicero and the triumvirate, Caesar in his own words and in a later account, and Augustus telling his own story.

concepts.title: Tradition
concepts.summary: A story handed down about the past without a record made at the time.

concepts.title: Exemplum
concepts.summary: A story told to show conduct a reader should copy or avoid.

concepts.title: Traditional date
concepts.summary: A date given by later writers for an event that nobody recorded when it happened.

concepts.title: Consul
concepts.summary: One of two magistrates elected each year, in charge of public business at Rome and of the army in the field.

concepts.title: Senate
concepts.summary: The council of former magistrates, which controlled money, foreign relations and advice to the magistrates.

concepts.title: Assembly
concepts.summary: A meeting of citizens that elects magistrates, passes laws and decides on war and peace.

concepts.title: Veto
concepts.summary: A tribune's power to stop an act by saying 'I forbid'.

concepts.title: Mixed constitution
concepts.summary: A system in which monarchic, aristocratic and popular elements check one another, as Polybius describes Rome's.

concepts.title: The two orders
concepts.summary: Patricians, the old governing families, and plebeians, the other citizens, who for generations could not hold the main offices.

concepts.title: Secession
concepts.summary: A refusal by the plebeians to serve or to stay in the city until their demands were met.

concepts.title: The Twelve Tables
concepts.summary: Rome's first written laws, traditionally dated to about 450 BCE.

concepts.title: Change and continuity
concepts.summary: What a period altered and what it left as it was; both need evidence.

concepts.title: Ally
concepts.summary: A self-governing Italian community tied to Rome by treaty, which sent troops when the consuls asked.

concepts.title: Citizen levy
concepts.summary: An army raised each year from citizens who own property, rather than hired soldiers.

concepts.title: Colony
concepts.summary: A settlement of Roman citizens planted in conquered land, joined to Rome by roads.

concepts.title: Hedged report
concepts.summary: A claim a writer passes on while signalling that he does not vouch for it, with words such as 'there is a story' or 'it is said'.

concepts.title: Partisan source
concepts.summary: A source written by someone on one side of the matter it describes.

concepts.title: War guilt
concepts.summary: The question of which side is to blame for starting a war.

concepts.title: Hedged number
concepts.summary: A figure given with a sign that the writer cannot vouch for it, such as 'are said to have been'.

concepts.title: Authority
concepts.summary: The earlier writer a historian names as the source of a claim.

concepts.title: Corroboration
concepts.summary: Support for a claim from a second source that did not get it from the first.

concepts.title: Moral explanation
concepts.summary: An explanation of events by the habits and character of a people or its leaders.

concepts.title: Proletariat
concepts.summary: The landless working poor of the city of Rome, as the textbook uses the word.

concepts.title: Interpretation
concepts.summary: An account that selects facts and weighs them to explain what happened.

concepts.title: Later account
concepts.summary: An account written long after the events, built on earlier sources, some of which it names.

concepts.title: Chain of testimony
concepts.summary: The line from an event to the reader: who saw it, who told whom, who wrote it down.

concepts.title: Tribune
concepts.summary: An official elected by the plebeians who could propose laws and stop the acts of others.

concepts.title: Client army
concepts.summary: An army whose soldiers are more loyal to their commander, who promises them pay and land, than to the state.

concepts.title: Proscription
concepts.summary: A published list of men whom anyone might kill, and whose property was seized.

concepts.title: Dictator
concepts.summary: An old office that gave absolute authority for a limited time to meet an emergency.

concepts.title: Conspiracy
concepts.summary: A secret plan by a group to seize power or overthrow the government.

concepts.title: Triumvirate
concepts.summary: A private alliance of three men; the first, in 60 BCE, joined Pompey, Crassus and Caesar.

concepts.title: Claimed impartiality
concepts.summary: A writer's statement that he has no interest in the matter, which is itself something he chose to say.

concepts.title: Commentary
concepts.summary: Caesar's own report of his campaigns, written in the third person for readers at Rome.

concepts.title: Count and census
concepts.summary: A figure Caesar gives from a list or count; the question is who made it.

concepts.title: Justification
concepts.summary: A reason a writer gives for an action, chosen to persuade.

concepts.title: Res Gestae
concepts.summary: Augustus's own list of what he had done, set up on bronze columns in Rome.

concepts.title: Principate
concepts.summary: The system Augustus created, in which a first citizen held power through the old offices.

concepts.title: Facade
concepts.summary: An outward form kept after the substance has changed.

lessons.title: Founding stories and what Livy knew
lessons.orientation: Tell a founding tradition from evidence for the events it describes, and say what Livy's telling of the early stories is good evidence of.
lessons.reviewLabel: Founding stories and what Livy knew

lessons.title: The constitution seen from outside
lessons.orientation: Say which body held which power in the middle Republic, and weigh Polybius's description by who he was and what he wanted to explain.

lessons.title: The Struggle of the Orders and the Twelve Tables
lessons.orientation: Use a narrative and a law code together to say what changed and what stayed the same in the early Republic, and what each is evidence of.
lessons.reviewLabel: The Struggle of the Orders and the Twelve Tables

lessons.title: How Rome came to rule Italy
lessons.orientation: Explain Roman expansion in Italy as a mix of conditions and policies with no master plan, and say what each source can and cannot show about it.
lessons.reviewLabel: How Rome came to rule Italy

lessons.title: Why the Second Punic War began
lessons.orientation: Separate the conditions, causes and trigger of the Second Punic War, and show where Livy's account takes Rome's side.
lessons.reviewLabel: Why the Second Punic War began

lessons.title: Hannibal in Italy and the numbers at Cannae
lessons.orientation: Read a casualty figure in an ancient source for who counted it and how sure the writer is, and compare two accounts of what Cannae did to Rome's allies.
lessons.reviewLabel: Hannibal in Italy and the numbers at Cannae

lessons.title: What empire did to Rome
lessons.orientation: Compare three explanations of the Republic's troubles, say which parts are fact, evidence or interpretation, and say what each writer could see from where he stood.

lessons.title: The Gracchi and a later biographer
lessons.orientation: Weigh what a biographer writing long after the events can know about motives, by tracing who each claim comes from and comparing a second account.
lessons.reviewLabel: The Gracchi and a later biographer

lessons.title: Marius, Sulla and soldiers who followed a general
lessons.orientation: Explain how soldiers' loyalty moved from the state to their commanders, separating what Sallust and Plutarch report from what the textbook concludes.
lessons.reviewLabel: Marius, Sulla and soldiers who followed a general

lessons.title: Catiline, Cicero and the first triumvirate
lessons.orientation: Read Sallust's account of Catiline for its author's purpose, check it against Plutarch, and say how Plutarch explains the road to civil war.
lessons.reviewLabel: Catiline, Cicero and the first triumvirate

lessons.title: Caesar in his own words and in Plutarch's
lessons.orientation: Read Caesar's own reports for their purpose and compare them with Plutarch's later account, including the scene at the Rubicon.
lessons.reviewLabel: Caesar in his own words and in Plutarch's

lessons.title: Augustus: the Republic restored, in his own words
lessons.orientation: Test Augustus's own account of his career against a later biographer and a textbook, and say what changed and what stayed in the constitution after 27 BCE.
lessons.reviewLabel: Augustus: the Republic restored, in his own words
